title: A predictive mechanism for plant cell-wall growth and mechanical sensing

concept.text: The innovation would be a causal explanation that predicts how a plant cell changes its growth when mechanical conditions change. It would connect forces acting on the cell wall, wall composition and remodeling, sensing associated with the cell membrane, cytoskeletal organization and gene regulation into experimentally testable feedback loops. The established foundation is that cell walls are central to plant growth and mechanics, and that wall stress and wall loosening cooperate to produce growth.

As a proposed research target, this account would explain both how mechanical conditions affect cellular activity and how the resulting changes in wall construction alter subsequent forces and growth. It would distinguish components that detect mechanical conditions directly from components that respond farther along the signaling pathway. In particular, microtubules should be tested as possible primary sensors or downstream responders in each biological context; their direct sensing role should not be assumed.

significance.text: Because cell walls help determine how plant cells expand and how plant form develops, a mechanism that prospectively predicts regulated wall growth across biological contexts would substantially advance the explanation of plant morphogenesis. Its significance would come from connecting physical constraints and cellular regulation in a causal account that can survive intervention, rather than merely describing associations between wall properties and growth. This is a conditional impact judgment grounded in the documented importance of walls to growth, morphogenesis and mechanics.

Potential downstream applications include designing plant materials with particular mechanical properties or directing crop architecture through controlled growth. These remain possibilities requiring additional engineering. As a scope inference, a successful account of wall mechanics would provide one important component of plant design, while developmental regulation, environmental responses and other biological processes would still affect whole-plant outcomes. Success in selected tissues would therefore establish useful predictive reach without establishing control over all plant form.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed breakthrough is an integrated mechanism that quantitatively links mechanical inputs to sensing, wall remodeling and growth, and predicts what happens when individual parts of that system are changed. The supplied review supports the wall-growth and cellular-regulation foundation, but its accessible preview does not establish complete feedback loops encompassing membrane-associated sensing, cytoskeletal organization and gene regulation. It also cannot establish which parts of that integration remain unresolved at the intended contemporary assessment date.

Scientific barriers to test include identifying the relevant sensing components in each context, distinguishing direct mechanical detection from secondary responses, and establishing the direction of causation within feedback loops. For example, a change in microtubule organization following a mechanical perturbation would not by itself show that microtubules detected the perturbation directly. Perturbations must separate sensing from effects on wall construction, cellular organization or the ability to grow.

Engineering requirements inferred from the research target include measuring forces and wall properties alongside growth at compatible spatial and temporal scales, connecting those measurements to wall composition and remodeling, and obtaining sufficiently selective interventions to test competing mechanisms. Predictive models would also need explicit biological boundaries: a mechanism calibrated in one tissue or species may require different parameters or additional components elsewhere. These are proposed requirements for evaluating the innovation, rather than a verified inventory of the field's remaining technical gaps.

current_state.text: Daniel J. Cosgrove’s review, “Structure and growth of plant cell walls,” was published online on 15 December 2023. Its abstract describes the physics of wall growth and cellular regulation through cellulose production, plasma-membrane proton pumps, expansins and hormones. It explains that wall stress and wall loosening cooperate in growth. This establishes a substantive mechanistic foundation for the proposed integration, but does not demonstrate that the full predictive sensing-and-growth mechanism described here has been achieved.

According to the supplied evidence review, the retained publisher HTML is a subscription preview containing the abstract, figure titles, references and back matter; the article body and figures are unavailable. The retained artifact was not marked as truncated and had no recorded extraction issues, but those facts do not make the inaccessible article content available. Reference titles identify relevant research directions without independently establishing their findings. The preview therefore cannot determine the completeness of existing mechanistic models or settle whether microtubules directly sense force.

The supplied freshness record is empty, so the evidence does not verify the state of the field as of 1 November 2026. The source index records retrieval on 11 November 2026, but retrieval of a 2023 review does not establish coverage of subsequent advances. This limits contemporary conclusions without invalidating the review's dated mechanistic account. The retained evidence also does not substantiate the earlier description of a sign-in redirect or a separate first-pass indexed text.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: in several explicitly selected tissues and species, measure mechanical conditions, wall properties and growth, then perturb individual candidate sensors and cytoskeletal components. A model specified before the outcome is measured should predict the direction, magnitude and timing of growth responses within declared tolerances. The protocol should define the biological contexts, measurement uncertainty and prediction tolerances in advance. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established community standards.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective growth predictions meet declared direction, magnitude and timing tolerances

completion_criteria.text: Proposed causal validation: use interventions and rescue experiments to distinguish direct sensing from downstream responses. A convincing rescue would restore a predefined growth response through the mechanism being tested, with controls that address alternative explanations such as a general loss of growth capacity. Tests should challenge competing accounts of the feedback loop, including the possibility that microtubules organize a response without serving as the primary sensor.
completion_criteria.label: Interventions and rescues distinguish direct sensing from downstream responses

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope requirements: independent experiments should reproduce the measurements, interventions and prospective predictions using documented protocols and accessible model specifications. Evaluation should include conditions beyond those used to fit the model and report failures alongside successes. Several tissues and species would establish demonstrated breadth; finite testing cannot establish literal universality. Claims about crop architecture or designed plant materials would require additional practical demonstrations beyond explaining cellular growth.
completion_criteria.label: Independent experiments reproduce predictions beyond model-fitting conditions and report failures

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: BOT-17, “Predictive control of plant cell-division planes and tissue patterning,” overlaps through the role mechanical conditions could play in organizing tissues. BOT-13 centers on wall growth, mechanical sensing and their feedback, while BOT-17 centers on division orientation and tissue patterning. Their predictions could interact, but predicting cell expansion does not by itself establish predictive control of division planes. The supplied BOT-17 title supports this broad comparison; its detailed mechanism and completion criteria were not provided.

Roster-based comparison: BOT-05, “Predictive plant biology from genome to whole-organism performance,” has a broader predictive ambition. BOT-13 could supply a mechanistic component connecting cellular regulation to growth and form. Whole-organism prediction would still require integration with processes outside wall mechanics, so the two entries retain distinct scopes.

Roster-based comparison: BOT-12, “A causal map of plant-wide communication and plasmodesmatal control,” concerns communication across the plant and control of intercellular connections. BOT-13 concerns how cells detect mechanical conditions and adjust wall growth. Signals involved in mechanical responses could connect the two research targets, but the supplied evidence does not establish a specific shared pathway or show that explaining one would resolve the other.

brief.title: Predicting how forces change plant cell growth
possible: Researchers could predict how a plant cell will grow when forces on it change. The explanation would connect the cell wall, its strong outer layer, to the cell’s force detection, internal organization and control of genes.
This could help researchers direct crop growth or design plant materials with particular mechanical properties.
why: Plant shape depends on how cells expand. Connecting physical forces to the cell’s growth controls would help explain how that shape develops and give plant researchers predictions they could test by changing individual parts of the system.

sources.showed: His review explains how forces within the wall and wall loosening work together to produce growth, and how cells regulate wall construction.
sources.cited_for: It explains the physical and cellular foundations of wall growth.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a complete mechanism that predicts growth from force detection through to wall rebuilding.

sources.showed: In Arabidopsis plants, impairing katanin reduced growth differences between neighboring cells. Katanin cuts microtubules, fibers in the cell’s internal scaffold, and helped cells respond to mechanical forces.
sources.quote:
This variability was strongly decreased in a mutant
impaired in the microtubule-severing protein katanin.
sources.cited_for: It links changes in the internal scaffold to mechanical responses and growth patterns.
sources.not_established: It does not establish that microtubules detect forces directly or predict growth across tissues and species.

sources.showed: In Arabidopsis shoots, microtubules responded to mechanical stress without FERONIA, a candidate wall-sensing protein. Reducing wall tension partly relieved defects caused by losing FERONIA.
sources.quote: In fact, when performing mechanical perturbations, we instead show that the expected microtubule response to stress does not require FER.
sources.cited_for: It shows that wall sensing and microtubule responses need not form a single chain.
sources.not_established: It does not identify what directly detects force in the microtubule response.

sources.who: Xin Liu, Liu Wang and colleagues
sources.showed: Under salt stress, FERONIA interacted with proteins that help microtubules reassemble. This connects a candidate wall sensor to the machinery involved in rebuilding the wall.
sources.quote: Furthermore, CC1 phosphorylation level is altered upon exposure to salt stress, which coincides with the changes of microtubule organization.
sources.cited_for: It connects salt exposure to phosphorylation, a chemical change to a protein, and changes in the internal scaffold.
sources.not_established: A pathway responding to salt does not establish a complete mechanism for predicting growth after mechanical changes.

shown: Researchers have established parts of the connection between forces, wall construction and growth. Uyttewaal’s team linked katanin to mechanical responses; Malivert’s team separated those responses from FERONIA; Liu and Wang’s team connected FERONIA to microtubule rebuilding under salt stress.
missing: A complete model would need to connect forces, their detection, wall rebuilding, internal organization and gene control to growth.
Selective experiments would need to separate direct force detection from later responses and general damage to growth.
Independent tests would need to establish where the predictions hold across tissues and species, and where they fail.

milestones.label: Growth predictions meet declared accuracy limits
milestones.explanation: A model would have to predict growth direction, size and timing within preset limits after targeted changes across selected tissues and species. This would test whether it predicts outcomes before they are measured.

milestones.label: Disruption and restoration distinguish sensing from later responses
milestones.explanation: Experiments would have to disrupt and restore a defined growth response while ruling out general loss of growth capacity. This would distinguish direct force detection from later responses, including those involving microtubules.

milestones.label: Independent tests reproduce predictions and report failures
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce measurements, interventions and predictions beyond the conditions used to fit the model, reporting failures too. This would establish its reliability and biological reach.

uncertain: Microtubules may detect forces directly, respond to other sensors, or play different roles in different tissues.
The tissues, species, prediction limits and criteria for a successful restoration of growth still need to be defined.
Useful predictions in selected tissues may not translate into control over whole-plant shape or practical plant materials.

page.title: Mechanochemical feedback model of plant cell growth
page.definition: A causal model predicts plant-cell expansion after mechanical or genetic perturbation. It connects wall mechanics and remodeling to membrane-associated sensing, microtubules (protein filaments that guide cellulose deposition), and gene regulation, including feedback from altered growth to mechanical stress.

goal.need: In Arabidopsis shoot meristems, impairing katanin, a protein that cuts microtubules, reduced growth anisotropy by 37%. In FERONIA-deficient seedlings treated with a cellulose-synthesis inhibitor, increasing agar from 0.7% to 2.5% reduced the cell-bursting index by 70% (16 seedlings per group). A predictive mechanism would explain how changes in mechanics and cellular regulation produce directional expansion or loss of cell integrity.

figures.caption: Growth anisotropy in Arabidopsis shoot apical meristems
figures.note: Anisotropy is dimensionless. Cells are nested within meristems. Results published on 13 April 2012.

statements.quote: Here we propose to identify the plant mechanotransduction pathways and investigate their role in development
statements.context: The project objective specifies Arabidopsis cell cultures, cotyledons and shoot apical meristems as experimental systems.

statements.quote: We will then integrate these biophysical mechanisms in multicellular development.
statements.context: The preceding objective concerns microtubule responses to mechanical stress and their interaction with cell-wall sensing.

completion.title: An independent laboratory verifies an integrated model's predictions of plant-cell growth.
completion.criterion: For one stated plant species, tissue and developmental stage, an independent laboratory tests a fixed causal model linking wall stress, wall composition and remodeling, membrane-associated sensing, microtubule organization and gene regulation. After mechanical and genetic perturbations excluded from model fitting, predicted expansion rate, direction and time course agree with measurements within their stated uncertainty. Interventions distinguish direct force sensing from downstream responses. This is an Atlas-defined test; no numerical accuracy or replication threshold is attributed to an outside body.
completion.basis: Searches of ERC project objectives, the plant-morphogenesis roadmap, mechanosensor evidence criteria, and plant-growth model benchmark, standard, prize and registered-protocol literature found no end-to-end completion test. Published goals support integrating sensing with development and testing models against perturbations. The criterion covers one specified biological context and requires independent experimental confirmation; it makes no claim of universality.

milestones.title: Plant-cell microtubules reorient after an experimental change in mechanical stress.
milestones.criterion: Compression or local cell ablation changes the mechanical stress field, and cortical microtubules reorient along the new maximum tensile-stress direction. On 12 November 2021, Malivert et al. reported alignment 7 hours after ablation in Arabidopsis cotyledons grown on 2.5% agar: array anisotropy reached 0.16 in wild type (220 cells) and 0.17 in fer-4 (203 cells). FERONIA was unnecessary for this response. These values describe observations, not a required anisotropy threshold.
milestones.set_by: Plant mechanobiology research community; stress-perturbation tests applied by Uyttewaal et al. and Malivert et al. in Arabidopsis shoots.
milestones.threshold_quote: Such a perturbation causes the cortical microtubules to reorient in the new maximal tensile stress direction

milestones.title: A plant membrane mechanosensor passes functional-necessity and autonomous force-response tests.
milestones.criterion: A candidate membrane protein is required for a mechanical response in its native biological context and, if claimed to act autonomously, retains force sensitivity in another cell or a reconstituted membrane. On 1 November 2018, Murthy et al. reported stretch-activated Arabidopsis OSCA1.2 channels in artificial lipid vesicles: conductance was 346 ± 13 pS in 200 mM KCl (8 membrane patches). This establishes autonomous channel activity, not its role in the complete wall-growth feedback loop; the conductance is not a milestone threshold.
milestones.set_by: Mechanotransduction research community; function and mimicry criteria summarized by Goodman, Haswell and Vásquez in their 2023 Rules of evidence. These criteria concern membrane proteins and do not establish direct sensing by microtubules.
milestones.threshold_quote: are broadly applicable to all mechanosensors: function and mimicry.

milestones.title: An integrated feedback model predicts plant-cell growth in new perturbation experiments.
milestones.criterion: The originating laboratory tests a fixed model of the complete feedback loop on new mechanical and genetic perturbations in one stated biological context; predicted growth rate, direction and time course agree with measurements within stated uncertainty. This integrated endpoint was not demonstrated in the located sources. A component result was published on 29 November 2024: wild-type CC1 largely rescued reduced seedling-stem elongation in Arabidopsis cc1 cc2 mutants under 120 mM NaCl for 9 days; phosphorylation-site variants failed to rescue it (more than 33 seedlings per group). Salt stress alone does not isolate a mechanical input.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; searches of ERC objectives, the plant-morphogenesis roadmap and model-validation literature found no published integrated milestone or numerical error tolerance. This operational criterion combines their stated research goals and perturbation-validation approach.

not_found: No plant-specific benchmark, standard, prize rule or registered protocol defining an end-to-end accuracy threshold was located.
No located source demonstrated independent experimental validation of the complete model specified in the completion criterion.
The supplied Nature Reviews article redirected to an inaccessible sign-in page.
The Hervieux et al. sepal-model paper could not be opened at its Max Planck repository.

results.finding: Wild-type Arabidopsis meristem microtubules aligned after approximately 0.1 N compression; sample size not specified.
results.detail: Compression was predicted to increase tensile-stress anisotropy parallel to the blades, and arrays showed a bias in that direction. The paper states that all experiments were repeated at least five times with comparable results.
results.quote:
As previously observed, this
method increased the level of CMT bundling in the WT cells,
leading to strongly anisotropic CMTs arrays, with a bias toward
the direction parallel to the blades ( Figures 4D and 4F) ( Hamant
et al., 2008).

results.finding: Growth-rate variability was lower in atktn1 than wild type: 607 and 410 cells, respectively; p < 0.001.
results.detail: The growth measurements support a prediction of the mechanical-feedback model. The model does not establish the complete specified feedback loop or predict expansion rate, direction and time course for new mechanical and genetic perturbations within stated uncertainty.
results.quote:
Furthermore, the mean local variability was signiﬁcantly lower
in the mutant (t test, p < 0.001).

results.finding: After ablation, wild-type cortical microtubule anisotropy reached 0.16 at 7 hours (220 cells).
results.detail: In Arabidopsis cotyledons grown on 2.5% agar, microtubules reoriented circumferentially around ablated cells, along the predicted maximum tensile-stress direction. The response also occurred in fer-4.
results.quote: It increased by 50% 7 hours later, consistent with the co-alignment of cortical microtubules with tensile stress

results.finding: In isoxaben-grown fer-4 hypocotyls, higher agar reduced the bursting index by 70% (16 samples per group).
results.detail: The result implicates FERONIA in maintaining mechanical integrity under stress, but does not establish that FERONIA directly senses force or demonstrate autonomous force sensitivity.
results.quote: When increasing the agar concentration to 2.5%, the bursting index in hypocotyls was reduced by 70% in isoxaben-grown seedlings, supporting our hypothesis

results.finding: In Arabidopsis cc1 cc2 mutants, wild-type CC1 largely rescued hypocotyl elongation under 120 mM NaCl; n > 33 seedlings per group.
results.detail: Phosphorylation-site variants failed to rescue growth. This is a component result: salt stress does not isolate mechanical input, and no fixed complete feedback model was tested against growth predictions.

results.finding: Venus flytrap FLYC1 in HEK-P1KO cells had half-maximal activation at 77.3 ± 4.0 mmHg (N = 9).
results.detail: FLYC1 produced stretch-activated currents in another cell type, but its necessity for a mechanical response in Venus flytrap was not tested. The authors also call for reconstitution to establish inherent mechanosensitivity.
